segments.title: THE FEW STONES THAT HOLD THE ROAD
segments.angle: What if I approached this with the Pareto Principle in mind?

sources.text: The Value of Time: Time magnifies the margin between success & failure. It will multiply whatever you feed it.
The Value of Time: We all have the same limited time in a day.
The Value of Time: At any given moment, you are doing what you most want to be doing.
The Value of Time: Time is the only separator between your past, present and future.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The donut can wait. The road cannot.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Picture a long road covered in small stones. Most of them are just stones. A few of them hold the whole road up.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Wait, is the road the stones, or the stones the road? Because I only see stones.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Stay with me. Every man has the same limited time in a day. Same hours. Same clock. Nobody gets extra.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Same clock, very different days. That part is true, and it stings a little.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The Pareto Principle says that a small slice of what we do brings most of the results. Most of the work goes nowhere. A thin part of it does nearly everything.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Mark the hour. Something important just got said.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Marking it. Still the same hour, narrator.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Time multiplies whatever you feed it. So feed it the small slice. The part of the day that moves the needle.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Noted. I would still feed it the slice you can finish, though. Big slices spoil on the desk.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The small slice is not always the easy slice. Often it is the hour you keep saying you will do tomorrow.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Yes. That is the hour that hurts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Time is the only separator between your past, present and future. Every choice of the small slice is a stone set down for the man ahead.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay, the stone comparison is doing a lot of work. But fine. The stone is real.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Picture him looking back, years from now, at the few stones he chose to lift. That is the road he walked.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He did not get there by lifting every stone. He got there by finding the few that counted.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Narrator, your turn. Name your small slice on air. Then name the one hour you will stop pushing to tomorrow.

segments.title: THE SNOWBALL HAS NO OPINION
segments.angle: Create a simple analogy or metaphor to explain the core concept of this note. What does this analogy reveal about its strengths or weaknesses?

sources.text: The Value of Time: Time magnifies the margin between success & failure. It will multiply whatever you feed it.
The Value of Time: It feels like such a slow burn, but it's exponential. It creeps up on you on a day to day basis, but when you zoom out, it's an instant.
The Value of Time: We never actually "don't have the time" to do something. It's just that we're actively choosing to do something else.
The Value of Time: Time is a magnifier of who you are now.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: My small slice is a plain sentence, read aloud before I start talking big. The hour I keep pushing to tomorrow is the hour I like least.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Picture a snowball at the top of a hill. It is small. It is cold. It does not look like much at all.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay, but what would he actually do on Monday?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He wrote it down plainly: it feels like such a slow burn, but it's exponential.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Slow at the top. Fast at the bottom. Same snow.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Time is a magnifier of who you are now. That is the snowball's secret. It picks up whatever you pack into it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Noted. I'll say it anyway: the snowball has no opinion. It rolls over a clean lawn and a muddy path the same way.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the crack in the picture. A snowball does not choose its hill. You do.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right, and that is the part he is pointing at. We never actually don't have the time. We pick the hill.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So the analogy is honest about the growing. It is quiet about the choosing. Time does not roll by itself. It rolls the way you point it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Noted. I still like the snowball. It shows the growing part. It hides the choosing part.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Every lesson in a notebook like this was paid for by a bad day. Somebody learned it the hard way, with cold hands.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Mm. Not every bad day gets a lesson, though. Only the ones you write down.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So write it down. The snowball keeps rolling whether you watch it or not.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And it grows fastest where the hill runs longest. Pick a long hill.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Pick your hill, then. Pack it with what you want to be.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Narrator, what is your snowball made of? Answer in an honest sentence.

segments.title: THE EXCUSE GETS CUT
segments.angle: What could I remove from this idea to make it simpler, cheaper, or more effective? (Instead of just adding)

sources.text: The Value of Time: We never actually "don't have the time" to do something. It's just that we're actively choosing to do something else.
The Value of Time: We all have the same limited time in a day.

The Value of Time: When we say we don't have time to do something, what we really mean is that we don't think it's a high enough priority compared to the things that we're choosing to do instead, whether that's watching YouTube or napping.
The Value of Time: It's literally just about being.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Honest answer, March. My snowball is made of waiting. Soft, cold, and heavy.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Good. Now we can work with it. Let's cut it down.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Today we cut. We do not add. We strip this note to the bone.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine. Start with the biggest word in it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Here it is. He wrote it plainly: "We never actually "don't have the time" to do something."

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That is the cut. Delete the phrase. I don't have time. Gone.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It sounds too easy. The best ideas in his notebook often do.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay, but what would he actually do on Monday?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: On Monday, a man stops saying the excuse. He says the true thing instead. I am choosing something else right now.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ha. So: I am choosing to scroll. Honest. Then stop.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Here is the cold part. Most of what we call no time is a choice we already made.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Wait, the cold part? Narrator, say it nicer.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: No. It is true. I am telling it anyway.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay. Then what is left when the words are gone?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Just this: "It's literally just about being." Nothing else. That is the whole lesson.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Mark the hour. I'm counting it out loud.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Every good book ends on a quiet page. This is the page where you put the excuse down.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Narrator, on Monday, what excuse are you cutting, and what will you do instead?

segments.title: THE SLOW SEASON HAS A VOICE
segments.angle: What is the opposite of this idea, and how could that also be valid?

sources.text: Progress in life is not linear, it's exponential.
We Own All Of Our Time: At any given moment, you are doing what you most want to be doing.
The Value of Time: Time magnifies the margin between success & failure. It will multiply whatever you feed it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Fine. I cut the idea that every hour has to climb. Growth is not a straight line.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Careful, narrator. You just wrote a rule and called it a curve.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Here is the opposite, and it is valid. Time multiplies whatever you feed it. So what if you feed it rest?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay, let me try it on me, out loud. This week I feed time nothing. A slow week. Hmm.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Noted. I still disagree. Moving on.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the whole trick of this note. It is loud on one side and quiet on the other.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Some days you do not get to pick the hour. Life sends it. The idea that you always own your time is strong. It is not always true.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He treats this idea like it is carved in stone. Still true.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Narrator, we are carving on phones now. Very ancient.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Every lesson in a notebook like this was paid for by a bad day. Somebody had to lose the argument first.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the opposite is valid when the bad day is the teacher. Rest is not the same as hiding.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Rest you choose is a choice. Hiding is a choice too, and it has a sound. You can hear the difference.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I can hear it. Loudly. Usually at the wrong hour of the night.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So here is the thing to carry out of this. The slow season can grow something too. The question is which kind of waiting you are doing.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Narrator, be honest. Which kind of waiting are you doing this week?

segments.title: THE BAG THAT HOLDS ONLY TIME
segments.angle: If I could only use 2 resources to solve this problem, what would they be?

sources.text: The Value of Time: Time magnifies the margin between success & failure. It will multiply whatever you feed it.
The Value of Time: At any given moment, you are doing what you most want to be doing.
The Value of Time: We all have the same limited time in a day.
The Value of Time: Time is the only separator between your past, present and future.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: This idea is simple. A man with a bag. Only time and choice inside it. Can he still climb the mountain?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Simple? Narrator, do not call it simple and walk off. Time is the multiplier. It will multiply whatever you feed it. So choice is the food.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Time takes the choice and makes it big. The sea does not notice a pebble. It notices the tide.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay, that one I am taking a victory lap for. Now tell me what he would actually do on Monday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Monday. He has the same day everyone has. The same hours. Nobody lacks the time.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Sure. Everyone says that, right up until they stop saying it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: At any given moment, you are doing what you most want to be doing.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Wait. That is harsh.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It is harsh. It is also free. If you are the one choosing, you are the one who can choose again.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Noted. I still think the road and the mountain are different walks.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Mark the hour. Something started here.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hour counted. Keep going.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So here is the whole bag. Time, which multiplies. And choice, which decides what goes in.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Time magnifies. Choice feeds it. That is the whole deal, and it is free.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That closes these notes. Thank you for walking the road with us.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Be who you need to be, now. Goodbye, notes.

segments.title: THE OLD STONE TYPED ON A PHONE
segments.angle: How was this problem (or a similar one) addressed in the past (e.g., 10, 50, 100 years ago)? What can be learned from previous attempts or contexts?

sources.text: Everything Is Subjective: There is no objective right or wrong. There are as many opinions in life as there are people. Some call it black. Others call it white. Everything is subjective.
Everything is Subjective: It's a fool's game to think there's any objective right or wrong, because there is none. Everything is subjective.
Everything is Subjective: Our attitude is like the lens in which we see the world through. A different lens effectively changes your entire reality.
Happiness And Gratitude: Happiness is simply a state of mind in which our thinking is pleasant most of the time.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Long before any phone was in anyone's hand, people argued about what was true. Some of the smartest men of their age were sure they had it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Smartest men of their age. Narrator, you are carving on stone again.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I am carving it on stone. Fine, it was typed on a phone. The cold part comes next.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then say the cold part. I can take it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Aristotle said the Earth sat at the center of everything. Everybody believed him, because he was so wise.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then a man named Galileo looked at the sky and said no.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Galileo was right about the Earth. He was also wrong about comets and the tides. Everybody believed him too.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the lesson is that smart people are wrong sometimes. Simple.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Do not say simple. March, that is a whole history of people being sure.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It is simple, and I will defend it. Small habits, small checks, and do not hang your whole self on one loud voice. Nobody writes a legend about a checklist, and it still saves the day.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Newton came after them and blew everyone's mind. He also spent years trying to turn metal into gold.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay, that one is funny. Noted.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: His own note says it plainly. Our attitude is like the lens in which we see the world through.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So a lens is a habit. You change it with small things, every day, not with one big speech.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And a different lens changes the whole world you see. Even the old stones.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The stones do not care. Monday does. So tell me, narrator, which lens are you changing before anything else? Answer me next time.

segments.title: THE GLASS IS STILL SOFT
segments.angle: If the world's leading expert on [Unrelated Field] looked at this, what nuance or advanced application might they see?

sources.text: Everything Is Subjective: Change the way you approach life and the lens in which you view the world, and the entire world changes accordingly.
Everything Is Subjective: A different lens effectively changes your entire reality.
Happiness And Gratitude: Happiness is simply a state of mind in which our thinking is pleasant most of the time.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: March asked which lens I change before anything else. Fair question. Picture a glassblower with a hot pipe in his hand.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Picture him. Now tell me what he does with it, narrator.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He does not wait for the glass to cool. He shapes it while it is still soft. Once it hardens, the shape stays.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay, that is the nuance I wanted. You do not fix the lens after it sets. You fix it while it is soft.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: His notebook says it plainly. A different lens effectively changes your entire reality. But the lens has to be soft to change.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Soft is the key word. Most people wait for the glass to go hard, then wonder why it will not bend.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Happiness is simply a state of mind in which our thinking is pleasant most of the time. That is the lens. You shape it on a normal Tuesday, not on the big day.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A normal Tuesday. Noted, narrator. And I am not saying it is easy.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: No. Easy would mean nothing is being shaped at all.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Easy is not in his notes, narrator. Only the lens, and how you approach life. Let's keep to that.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Mark the hour. Something started the moment he held the pipe still.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I am not counting that out loud. Fine. I am counting it now.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Here is the twist. The glassblower does not make the lens clear. The heat does. The soft time does the real work.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hot glass does not care who you are. It just stays where you put it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the thing I most want said today.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then here is my question. Narrator, what do you shape before the glass sets on Monday?

segments.title: THE RULE THAT COSTS EVERYTHING
segments.angle: What could I remove from this idea to make it simpler, cheaper, or more effective? (Instead of just adding)

sources.text: Everything Is Subjective: There is no objective right or wrong. There are as many opinions in life as there are people.
Feelings Do Not Require Reason: If you wait until you "deserve" to think pleasant thoughts, you're likely to think unpleasant thoughts regarding your own unworthiness.
Feelings Do Not Require Reason: Happiness is not a moral issue, anymore than the circulation of blood is a moral issue.
Everything Is Subjective: So don't get too caught up in what's right or wrong.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Nothing. Right away, I cut.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Good. Cut what, exactly? Show me the fat.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The fat is the rule. You wait until you deserve a good thought.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And while you wait, you think the bad thoughts about your own worth. That is the cost. It is cheap to keep and expensive to live with.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So cut it. Happiness is not a moral issue.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right. Blood does not ask permission to move. Happiness works the same way.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Less rule. More looking. Everything is subjective, so there is no test to pass.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I like that. There is no objective right or wrong, so there is nothing to earn.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Think of it as a snow day.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine. But do not hide in the snow. Do not get too caught up in what is right or wrong. Just look.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The lens is free. It always was. He only had to stop charging himself for it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That is the cheapest version of the idea, and the best one. I will take it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then here is my question. March, what would you cut from your own rules today?

segments.title: THE LENS CAN HIDE A MAN
segments.angle: What are the potential ethical implications or societal consequences (positive or negative) of this idea if widely adopted? How could it be misused?

sources.text: Everything Is Subjective: There is no objective right or wrong.
Everything Is Subjective: So who's to say that we're right and they're wrong?
Feelings Do Not Require Reason: Happiness is not a moral issue, anymore than the circulation of blood is a moral issue.
Everything Is Subjective: Change the way you approach life and the lens in which you view the world, and the entire world changes accordingly.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You asked what I would cut. Easy. The rule that says I have to be sure about everything.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Picture a room where every person says, I am right. And every one of them means it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That is a Tuesday in any comment section. Okay, keep going.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: There is no objective right or wrong. A man can hear that sentence and feel free. Or he can hear it and hide.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hide is the word. That is the ugly misuse. My truth, your truth, and nobody gets hurt because it is all just a lens.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He wrote it plainly: happiness is not a moral issue. A good feeling is not a court.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So it works both ways. Feeling good does not make you good. He is careful about that part.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Careful is the word. Some lessons are only that: a warning written in small print.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I disagree with your big stone voice. Noted. Moving on.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Here is the good side. If nothing is set in stone, we judge less. We listen more. That is kindness with room in it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay, that one I am taking a victory lap for. Who is to say you are the right one, though? Maybe you are the one who needs to listen.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Feelings do not require reason. So the test is not how you feel. The test is what your choices do to other people.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay, but what would he actually do on Monday? When someone is hurt, does he shrug and say it is all subjective?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The notes are about change: change the way you approach life, and the lens changes. A lens changes what you see. Whether your hands follow is the question the notes leave open.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I like that. Put it on the wall, right above the rule I am cutting.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Every idea that sounds too easy has a hard edge. This one's edge is what you do next. March, when the lens shows you that you were wrong, what do you do?

segments.title: THE LENS IN THE SEA VILLAGE
segments.angle: How would I explain this idea if I had to tell it like a children's fairy tale?

sources.text: Everything Is Subjective: I may not be able to change the world, but I can change the way I see the world.
Everything Is Subjective: A different lens effectively changes your entire reality.
Everything Is Subjective: There is no objective right or wrong.
Feelings Do Not Require Reason: Happiness is simply a state of mind in which our thinking is pleasant most of the time.
Smile To Be Happy: When you smile, your brain automatically assumes you're having a good time.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Long ago, in a village by the sea, there lived a man who thought the world was too big to change. So he stopped trying before he began.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That is a sad start for a fairy tale. Okay, keep going. Let's see if the lens shows up.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A lens came to his door. It was old, and it said only this: I may not be able to change the world. But I can change the way I see it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay, I love a talking lens. Fine, but what does he eat for breakfast on Monday?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So he looked at the thing that bothered him most. He asked the lens a question. A different lens effectively changes your entire reality, and his did.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The village had a rule. There is no objective right or wrong. Sounds like a nice rule, which is exactly the warning.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Every house had its own window. Every window showed a different truth. Nobody was lying. Nobody was finished either.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Noted. I still think the easy-sounding ideas are the most dangerous, and also the best. Keep going.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the man saw that he had been waiting. Waiting to feel he deserved a good day. He wrote it down plainly: Happiness is simply a state of mind in which our thinking is pleasant most of the time.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: There it is. That line is the whole fairy tale, plain as a stone. No prize at the end. Just the thinking.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He smiled at the sea. Not because the sea was calm. Because his brain, the old wise animal, decided it was a good day.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Careful, narrator. You are about to turn a smile into magic.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Magic is a big word, March.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then say it small. Mark the hour, and I will count it out loud. Okay, it counts. The sea got smaller.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of the lens, and the end of these notes. Put the sea on the wall, and let the rest of the year do the work.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Good night, sea. Good night, lens. On Monday, he smiles first, and then he thinks.

segments.title: THE CLERK WHO FILES EVERYTHING
notes: How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences
segments.angle: How might I look at this problem from an entirely different perspective?

sources.text: How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Your nervous system cannot tell the difference between an imagined experience and a real one.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Mental practice is as powerful as actual practice.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: The brain learns from repetition. If you hear something enough times, your brain will start to believe it's true.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: When visualising, you must make these images as detailed and vivid as possible.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Whatever you believe about yourself, you are right.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Picture a clerk in a grey office, the kind with no windows. Every file that lands on his desk, he files. He never checks if it is true.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That clerk is your nervous system. Noted, and I am saying it before you make him sound lazy. He is not lazy. He is just very literal.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Stop looking at the world for a minute. Look at the desk. From there, a vivid picture and a real day look exactly the same.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That is the entirely different view. We always ask, is the world true? The clerk asks, what did I receive? Totally different question.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then repetition does the rest. Say a thing enough times and the clerk starts to believe it. He does not check the source.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So if you keep filing I am slow, he will hand you slow. He is not being mean. He is being obedient.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So write the file yourself. Clean and vivid, the way you would describe a room you love. Small details. The light. The sound of the door.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Mental practice is as powerful as actual practice. The clerk cannot tell the court from the gym. He just sees a good file.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Mark the hour. A man can look at his own mind the way the clerk looks at paper, and see that it was never the world. Only the file.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hour marked. I am counting it out loud, and it is a long count. Okay, I need to push. Would the clerk really stamp anything you gave him?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: On Monday, he files a new one. The smell of the coffee. The weight of the pen. He files it again, and again, until it sticks.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Noted. I still think the clerk is too calm. But I will let him be calm.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The notebook holds a plain lesson. Whatever you believe about yourself, you act on. So check which file you keep.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Some pages only make sense when you are the one holding the pen.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then here is my question, narrator. If the clerk is always the one holding the pen, who is holding yours?

segments.title: THE ASSUMPTION IN THE PEN
notes: How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences
segments.angle: What assumptions am I making in this idea?

How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Your nervous system cannot tell the difference between an imagined experience and a real one.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Whatever you believe about yourself, you are right.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: The brain learns from repetition.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Think and speak only the grandest narrative for yourself.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: How we see ourselves and how we see the world effectively is the truth as far as we're individually personally concerned.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Nobody holds mine, March. I write the page, and then I believe the page.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Your page is a good page. Still, this note makes some big claims without checking them.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Which claims? He wrote that the nervous system cannot tell the difference between imagined and real.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Every time is a big assumption. The body reacts to what it feels. Does that mean it cannot tell? That is a different sentence.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A sure voice, and then a question he never asked. Mark the hour.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That is another one for the tally. Mark the hour, narrator, and I count it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Let me try a title. The Keeper of Quiet Rules. He would look good on a stone.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: No. He is not the keeper of anything. Veto. Keep typing.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Noted. I still say the claim about belief is the big one.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Whatever you believe about yourself, you are right.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That is the assumption I would check on a Monday. The note says if you believe you are eating worms, you gag. Fine. But are you right about yourself? Or only awake?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The body follows the belief, that is his claim. True in a gag. What about a bad belief about your own voice?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then the belief is not the truth. It is the story the body is told. A big difference.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He wrote that the brain learns from repetition. Say a thing enough times and it becomes fact.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Repetition is not proof, narrator. It is practice. Practice can be wrong too.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Think and speak only the grandest narrative for yourself.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Only the grandest? What if the grandest story is a lie? Check it before you say it out loud.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: How we see ourselves is the truth as far as we're individually personally concerned. That is the assumption under all of it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So here is my dare to you, narrator. Which belief in this note have you never checked? Bring it back to me next scene.

segments.title: THE LEMON THE BODY BELIEVES
notes: How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences
segments.angle: Simplify this concept so a five-year-old could grasp the basic principle. What is the absolute essence?

sources.text: How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Your nervous system cannot tell the difference between an imagined experience and a real one.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Your nervous system reacts simply to what you think or imagine to be true.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Vividly imagining a situation is literally the same as experiencing it, as far as your brain's concerned.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: The brain learns from repetition. If you hear something enough times, your brain will start to believe it's true.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Repeat what you want to believe every day, multiple times a day. And soon, your actions and behaviour will follow.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Whatever you believe about yourself, you are right.
How Our Brains Interpret Imagined And Real Experiences: Think and speak only the grandest narrative for yourself.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: March, you asked which belief I never checked. Here is the simplest one. The mind cannot tell a real lemon from a pictured one.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Close your eyes. Picture a lemon. Okay, my mouth just did something. That is the whole lesson, honestly.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The body does not ask if it is real. It reacts to what the mind believes, and that is all.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So a little kid can do it. Picture the thing well, and the body thinks you did it. Simple.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The brain learns by hearing things again. Say a thing enough, and the brain starts to nod along.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Repeat the good thing every day, and the body follows. Boring, but I love boring. Small daily wins.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Whatever you believe about yourself, you are right. The essence is that line. Nothing fancy.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Noted. Mostly noted. Because you can believe a bad thing too, and the body goes along with that. Same rule, either way.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Think and speak only the grandest story about yourself. That is the whole essence, put in one line.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Grand is fine. Daily is better. A little kid would say: say the nice thing, then go do it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The note does not dress it up. That is why it sticks. Plain words, true every time.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay, narrator, one last thing. Which belief about yourself will you say out loud tomorrow? Tell me. Then I will tell you if it worked.
